name: Rosa Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead joiner for Albright's, a small builder that does old buildings: farmhouses, cottages, and at the moment the roof and the gallery stairs in a chapel up the valley. I'm there by half seven. Most days I'm cutting oak by hand, splicing new timber into rotten beams, making sash windows that match ones put in a hundred and fifty years ago. My dad was a carpenter and his dad too, and I use some of their chisels.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love taking something old and making it last another hundred years. When the chapel warden came up and touched the new stair rail and said it felt like the old one, that was my whole week. What wears me out is the money. Old-building work is slow and clients always want it cheaper. I'm the best joiner Albright's has, and I'm still paid less than people doing new houses in the city. My fiancé Mateo and I are getting married next summer, and every spare penny's going into that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's how it should be. Machines are for helping, not for running things. I'd say it after Mass to my brothers, probably, and they'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life goes on as planned. Wedding next summer, keep working, maybe a little house in a few years. I'd be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on just as I am. Work hard, save for the wedding, keep my head down. I wouldn't change a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI at all. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't need it. I've got my hands, my dad's square and a pencil. My youngest brother keeps telling me to ask it things. I tell him to ask Dad instead, he knows more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With the wedding coming, how tight are things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. About three weeks of money after the wedding deposit for the church hall. My mum's doing the food with my aunts, so that saves a lot. We'll manage, families do.

S0.say: I'd say good, that's how it should be: machines are for helping, not for running things. I'd say it to my brothers after Mass.
S0.think: It means my life goes on as planned, with the wedding next summer and maybe a little house in a few years. I'd be glad.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as now, working hard and saving for the wedding. Changes nothing about her work or plans.
S0.quote: I've got my hands, my dad's square and a pencil.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa's identity is rooted in family, faith and a craft passed down from her father and grandfather. She sees no need for AI tools. Her money is stretched by the wedding, but her family's help is a real cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should work hard and adapt, like they always have. But I'd also say don't throw away skills that took generations to learn. You can't download a chisel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my kind of work is safer than most. No robot is going to splice a beam in a chapel roof. But if new houses get cheaper with robots, fewer people will pay for old-fashioned work like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on at Albright's and try to save more, maybe twenty-five a week after the wedding. I wouldn't learn the AI things. I'd rather be the best at the old way than average at the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A little shadow, but I'd trust it would work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said old buildings protect you. Do you really believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. But Mr Albright's sixty-two. If he retires and the firm closes, there's nobody else doing this round here. Then I'd be doing kitchen fittings at the retail park, or nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, mostly, for selling these things like magic. And people who want everything cheap and quick. Good work takes time and costs money. But I don't think the government should fix it with handouts. That's not the answer.

S1.say: I'd say people should work hard and adapt as they always have, but not throw away skills that took generations to learn. You can't download a chisel.
S1.think: My kind of work is safer than most, because no robot is splicing a beam in a chapel roof. But if new houses get cheaper, fewer people will pay for old-fashioned work like mine.
S1.do: Keeps working at Albright's and tries to save about 25 a week after the wedding. Refuses to learn AI tools, preferring to be the best at the old way.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a small shadow, but trusting it will work out.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the best at the old way than average at the new one.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa trusts her heritage niche but sees its weak point: one ageing boss and no other local firm. She blames tech companies and cheap-minded clients, and rejects state handouts as the fix. Her resistance to new tools is a matter of pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong. Men in big companies decided this for everyone, and nobody asked us. I'd say that to anyone, and I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. Two years. I've got three weeks of money and a wedding. Even old buildings would get robots eventually, if they're as good as you say. I don't know what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything. I'd move the wedding to a small one at the church with lunch at my parents' house instead of the hall. Mateo and I would move in with his parents for a while to save rent. And I'd lean on my family, my brothers have said they'd help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night, and I never sleep badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would get smaller, not cancelled. We'd still get married, God willing. Just in my mum's garden with forty people instead of a hundred and twenty. Honestly, my gran would prefer that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want handouts. Would you take government help if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes, but I'd hate it. I'd rather my brothers helped, or the parish. Taking government money would feel like failing. I know that's maybe old-fashioned. It's how I was raised.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong that people in big companies decided this for everyone without asking us. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd pray about it.
S2.think: I'd be frightened: two years, three weeks of money and a wedding. Even old buildings would get robots eventually, and I don't know what else I'd do.
S2.do: Cuts all spending and shrinks the wedding to a church service and lunch at her parents' house. Moves in with her fiancé's parents to save rent and leans on her brothers and parish for support.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at night when she normally sleeps well.
S2.quote: It would get smaller, not cancelled. We'd still get married, God willing.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast picture Rosa's fallback is family and faith, not the state, which she would accept only reluctantly. The wedding shrinks but stays, which tells you what matters most. Her trust in her heritage niche gives way under the AGI premise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so families need to get ready. Pay off debts, look after each other. That's what I'd tell my cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives me time to get married properly and save a bit. But I'm not sure five years is enough for someone like me to become someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have the wedding as planned, but cheaper. Then save every week I can, maybe thirty, and pay off the van. Keep at Albright's while there's work and help Mr Albright find jobs, because if his firm goes, I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel it coming like winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be married by then. Would you think about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want to. But I'd want to wait and see first. I don't want to bring a baby into the world just as I lose my job. That would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new, given five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something close to what I know, like teaching carpentry at the college, if they still need teachers. But no, not computers. I'd be no good at that, and I wouldn't enjoy it.

S3.say: I'd say we've been warned, so families need to get ready, pay off debts and look after each other. That's what I'd tell my cousins.
S3.think: It gives me time to get married properly and save a bit. But I'm not sure five years is enough for someone like me to become someone else.
S3.do: Holds a cheaper wedding as planned, then saves about 30 a week and pays off the van. Stays at Albright's and helps her boss find work, and delays starting a family.
S3.feel: Anxious, feeling it coming like winter.
S3.quote: I don't want to bring a baby into the world just as I lose my job.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Rosa time for the wedding but not, she thinks, to remake herself. She would consider teaching carpentry but rules out anything on computers. Her biggest change is delaying children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and good craftsmen will always find work with people who care about quality. I believe that, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it lets me have the life I planned for a while. Married, maybe a baby. But at the end of it, I'd still be thirty-seven with a trade the robots can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Albright's and start doing my own small jobs on Saturdays, restoring windows and stairs for people who love old houses. I'd save everything from that. I'd want to build my own name, so people ask for Rosa, not just a builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quieter. More like a worry you carry than one that keeps you up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned private work. What's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who own old houses and want them done right. The priest's house, a couple of farmhouses. They'd pay for a person who cares. That might still be true when the robots come, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years from now, children might be small when it hits. Does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. I'd be thinking about school shoes and the mortgage just when my work dries up. So I'd try to have savings by then, real savings. And I'd want Mateo in a job that's safe, maybe at the school.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, and good craftsmen will always find work with people who care about quality. I mostly believe that.
S4.think: It lets me have the life I planned for a while, married and maybe a baby. But at the end, I'd still be thirty-seven with a trade the robots can do.
S4.do: Keeps working at Albright's and starts Saturday restoration jobs on windows and stairs for owners of old houses, saving all of it. Builds her own name so clients ask for her by name.
S4.feel: Anxious but quieter, a worry she carries rather than one that keeps her up.
S4.quote: I'd want to build my own name, so people ask for Rosa, not just a builder.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Rosa bets on reputation and private clients who value craft, a free-market answer that fits her views. She keeps worrying because the timing would collide with young children and a mortgage. She still would not touch AI tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time, no money, a wedding to pay for. What would help is apprenticeships and jobs that keep real craftspeople working, like paying people to restore old buildings properly. Not handouts. Work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. Nobody asks about that. When you don't know what's coming, the church and your family are what you lean on. That matters more round here than any government plan.

headlineQuote: No robot is going to splice a beam in a chapel roof.
portrait: Rosa is a 27-year-old lead joiner for a small heritage builder, restoring old houses and a chapel with her father's and grandfather's chisels. She is engaged to Mateo, with a wedding next summer eating most of her three weeks of savings, and she never uses AI. Her faith, family and pride in craft shape every answer. She is calm if AI fizzles and only uneasy in steady change, trusting old buildings to protect her, but alarmed at AGI in two years, when she would shrink the wedding and lean on family rather than the state. With more time she would build her own name through private restoration work while delaying children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, with no time, no money and a wedding to pay for.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and paid work that keeps real craftspeople busy, such as restoring old buildings properly, rather than handouts.
